questions.stem: What does one minute of latitude equal?
questions.explanation: One minute of latitude is one nautical mile, which is exactly 1852 m by international agreement. A statute mile is 1609 m and a cable is a tenth of a nautical mile.

questions.stem: How is a position in BC waters correctly written?
options: 49 degrees 10.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 40.0 minutes W
123 degrees 40.0 minutes W, 49 degrees 10.0 minutes N
49 degrees 10.0 minutes S, 123 degrees 40.0 minutes E
49.10 degrees N, 123.40 degrees W, meaning degrees and minutes
questions.explanation: Latitude comes first, then longitude, and BC is in north latitude and west longitude. Writing 49.10 degrees means 49 and a tenth of a degree, which is 49 degrees 6 minutes, not 49 degrees 10 minutes.

questions.stem: At 49 degrees N, a leg runs due east for 10.0 nm. If someone wrongly measured it on the longitude scale, about how many minutes would they read? (cos 49 degrees = 0.656)
questions.explanation: Difference of longitude = departure / cos latitude = 10.0 / 0.656 = 15.2 minutes. A minute of longitude is only 0.656 nm at 49 degrees, which is why the longitude scale cannot measure distance. 6.6 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

questions.stem: A lighthouse bears 306 degrees true from your ship. What is the bearing of the ship from the lighthouse?
questions.explanation: The reciprocal is 180 degrees different: 306 - 180 = 126. 054 is 360 - 306, a mirror image and not a reciprocal, and the others are 90-degree slips.

questions.stem: A buoy bears 247 degrees true from you. What is the bearing of your ship from the buoy?
questions.explanation: 247 + 180 = 427, which is more than 360, so subtract 360 to get 067. Directions never exceed 360. 113 is 360 - 247, and 157 is 247 - 90.

questions.stem: Two points: A is at 49 degrees 00.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 20.0 minutes W. B is 15.0 minutes of latitude north and 40.0 minutes of longitude east of A. The mean latitude is about 49 degrees (cos = 0.656). What is the distance from A to B, to the nearest 0.1 nm?
questions.explanation: Departure = 40.0 x 0.656 = 26.2 nm. Distance = square root of (15.0 squared + 26.2 squared) = square root of (225 + 687) = 30.2 nm. 42.7 results from using 40 minutes as miles, 55.0 adds 15 and 40, and 26.2 is only the departure.

questions.stem: You steam 10.0 nm due east at latitude 60 degrees N. By how many minutes of longitude does your longitude change? (cos 60 degrees = 0.5)
questions.explanation: Difference of longitude = departure / cos latitude = 10.0 / 0.5 = 20.0 minutes. Only at the equator does a minute of longitude equal a mile.

questions.stem: How is a course of seven degrees true correctly written?
questions.explanation: Directions are measured clockwise from north and always written with three figures, so 007, 047, 310.

questions.stem: Over what range do latitude and longitude run?
options: Latitude 0 to 180 degrees and longitude 0 to 90 degrees
Both 0 to 360 degrees measured clockwise from north
Latitude 0 to 90 degrees east or west and longitude 0 to 180 degrees north or south
Lat 0-90 N or S; long 0-180 E or W
questions.explanation: Latitude is measured north or south of the equator to a maximum of 90 degrees at the poles. Longitude is measured east or west of the Greenwich meridian to 180 degrees. Directions, not positions, run to 360.

questions.stem: You lift 8.0 nm on the dividers from a leg that lies near the middle of a Mercator chart. How do you check the length?
options: Place the dividers on the latitude scale at the side, level with the leg, and count minutes
Place the dividers on the longitude scale along the top and count minutes
Place the dividers on the latitude scale at the lowest edge of the chart, since it is the base line
Count the squares between the meridians
questions.explanation: One minute of latitude is one nautical mile, and on a Mercator chart the length of a minute of latitude changes with latitude, so use the part of the side scale level with your work.

questions.stem: How many metres are in one international nautical mile?
questions.explanation: The nautical mile is exactly 1852 m. 1609 m is the statute mile and 1760 is the number of yards in a statute mile.

questions.stem: You are at 49 degrees 05.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W and steam 22.0 nm on a course of 180 degrees true. What is your new position?
options: 49 degrees 27.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W
48 degrees 43.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 52.0 minutes W
48 degrees 58.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W
48 degrees 43.0 minutes N, 123 degrees 30.0 minutes W
questions.explanation: A due south run changes latitude only: 22.0 nm is 22.0 minutes, and 49 degrees 05.0 minutes minus 22.0 minutes is 48 degrees 43.0 minutes. Longitude is unchanged. The first answer goes north, and the third subtracts 7.
